chunks: "At the lowest level a timer is just a counter built from flip-flops, plus a comparator. The counter is a register of, say, 16 flip-flops with an incrementer in front of it.
On each clock edge the register loads its own value plus one.
A prescaler in front of it is also just a small counter that produces an enable pulse every N clocks, so the main counter only advances every Nth cycle.
Then there are comparators. A compare register holds a value you wrote, and a digital comparator, XNOR on each bit and an AND of the results, checks if the counter equals it.
When it matches, you set a flag flip-flop. That flag can raise an interrupt, toggle an output pin through a small logic block, or reset the counter, which is how reload works.
For input capture, an external pin goes through a two-flip-flop synchroniser, an edge detector, and the edge pulse loads the counter value into a capture register in one clock.
The software side is just memory-mapped registers. The CPU writes the prescaler, reload and compare values over the bus, and reads the count back.
Real designs add details like a shadow register so a new reload takes effect only at the update event, to avoid glitchy periods."
